system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2128-11-28 21:58:00 to 2128-11-30 13:23:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and gastroparesis was admitted for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy due to chronic cholecystitis and right upper quadrant pain. During the same operation, a laparoscopic appendectomy was performed due to uncertain appendiceal findings. The surgeries were uncomplicated. Postoperatively, pain was managed with IV and then oral morphine, with adjustments made for his opioid tolerance. He advanced to a regular diet by postoperative day two, ambulated well, and had no nausea or complications. His diabetes was managed with continued insulin, and his medications were updated, including increased duloxetine and simvastatin doses. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up scheduled in one month and detailed instructions on incision care, activity restrictions, and warning signs to monitor.
problems: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ man with right upper quadrant pain, status post
cholecystectomy and appendicitis one week ago.  Question of perforation,
abscess, complication of operation.

TECHNIQUE:  CT abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast.  Coronal and
sagittal reformatted images provided.

COMPARISON:  Compared to CT abdomen and pelvis from ___.

FINDINGS:  There is no focal consolidation or pleural effusion.

The liver is unremarkable.  There is no intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation. 
The patient is status post interval cholecystectomy and surgical clips are
seen in the gallbladder fossa.  There is an area of fluid, measuring 1.9 x 1.6
x 1.6 cm, in the surgical bed, in the region of the previous gallbladder
fundus.  No discrete wall is seen surrounding this collection.  The common
bile duct is prominent, which can be seen post-cholecystectomy.  The spleen
and adrenal glands are unremarkable.  Pancreas is again densely calcified with
prominence of the pancreatic duct, consistent with chronic pancreatitis.  The
kidneys enhance symmetrically and excrete contrast symmetrically with no
evidence of hydronephrosis.  There are small tiny hypodensities in the right
kidney, too small to characterize.  There is no bowel dilatation, pneumatosis,
free air, or free fluid.  There are no pathologically enlarged lymph nodes in
the retroperitoneum or mesentery.  The abdominal aorta is of normal caliber.

CT PELVIS:  Diverticula of the cecum are noted.  The rectum, and sigmoid are
unremarkable. There is no bowel obstruction. There are small diverticula in
the cecum.  Urinary bladder is distended.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions are seen.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Status post interval cholecystectomy.  Area of fluid in the surgical bed,
as above, without discrete wall, of unclear etiology, may be postoperative,
although biloma not entirely excluded.
2.  Pancreatic calcifications and ductal prominence consistent with chronic
pancreatitis.

Findings posted on the ED dashboard.

Addendum:

Additional information has been obtained from CareWeb Clinical Lookup since
the approval of the original report. Reason for exam should also state loss of
consciousness.

HISTORY:  ___ man with question of seizure.

Evaluate for intracerebral hemorrhage or mass.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial images were obtained through the brain.  No
intravenous contrast was administered.

COMPARISON:  Compared to CT head ___.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of acute hemorrhage, or shift of normally
midline structures.  There is no large acute vascular territorial infarct. The
gray-white matter differentiation is preserved.  There is no evidence of
hydrocephalus.  The ventricles and sulci are unremarkable.  The visualized
paranasal sinuses are clear.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial process.

Please note that MRI is more sensitive for subtle masses, if there is clinical
concern.

HISTORY:  Dilated common bile duct after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Concern
for retained stone.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images of the abdomen acquired on
a 1.5 Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and
after the uneventful IV administration of 0.1 mmol/kg gadolinium-DTPA.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations and subtraction images were generated on an
independent workstation.

MR OF THE ABDOMEN WITH IV GADOLINIUM (MRCP):  Susceptibility artifact from
cholecystectomy clips is noted.  There is mild extrahepatic bile duct
dilatation with the common duct measuring 9 mm with normal smooth distal
tapering.  There is no evidence of choledocholithiasis or obstructing mass
lesion.  Note is made of aberrant drainage of the right posterior bile duct
into the left main intrahepatic bile duct, an anatomic variant. No
intrahepatic biliary dilatation is present.

 The pancreatic duct is irregular and mildly dilated to 4 mm.  Multiple small
pancreatic duct side branches are noted.  Overall pancreatic parenchymal bulk
is diminished.  These findings are consistent with the patient history of
prior pancreatitis.  

Compared to the recent CT, there has been no change in an approximately 2.4 x
2.0 cm nonenhancing well-circumscribed focus of fluid signal intensity near
the gallbladder fossa, likely small amount of free fluid in the surgical bed. 
There are no concerning hepatic lesions.  

The spleen, adrenal glands, left kidney, stomach, and loops of bowel are
unremarkable. There is a small cyst of the right kidney.  There is no
lymphadenopathy or ascites.  The imaged lung bases are notable for dependent
lower lobe atelectasis and very small bilateral pleural effusions.  

There is no concerning bone marrow signal abnormality.  A small focus of
hyperintense T2- weighted signal of the bone marrow at L2 is compatible with
hemangioma.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations and subtraction images were essential in
evaluation of the biliary tree and pancreatic duct.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Mild bile duct dilatation probably related to prior cholecystectomy.  No
evidence of choledocholithiasis or obstructing lesion.

2.  Mild dilatation and irregularity of the pancreatic duct and diminished
pancreatic parenchymal bulk explained by prior pancreatitis.

3.  Small bilateral pleural effusions and dependent atelectasis of the lower
lobes, incompletely visualized.

4.  Minimal amount of fluid within the gallbladder fossa, likely
post-surgical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in after passing out earlier today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was at my cousin’s house visiting, and I just blacked out in the bathroom. I remember feeling dizzy and then nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was there any jerking or shaking before you passed out? Anyone say you might have had a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My cousin said I kind of stiffened up and my arms twitched. But I don’t think I was fully seizing. I’ve had that before, but sometimes it’s just stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. You were discharged from surgery about a week ago—cholecystectomy and appendectomy, right? How have you been feeling since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I’ve had this pain in my right upper belly, worse than before surgery. And I’ve been vomiting—yellow stuff, not bloody. It’s been going on since I got home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever? We heard you said it went up to 102 last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt really warm. I took some Tylenol and it came down, but I’ve been shaky and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. We’ve checked your labs. Your white blood cell count is a bit high, which suggests some inflammation, but no signs of a severe infection yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the surgery? Could something be wrong in there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your abdomen. There’s a small fluid collection near the surgical site, but it doesn’t look like an abscess. It could be normal post-op changes. We also saw your bile duct is a little dilated, which is common after gallbladder removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stones or blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the MRI we did shows no retained stones or blockages. Your pancreas looks stable—still showing signs of chronic damage, but nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough with pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also scanned your brain because of the fainting. No bleeding, no stroke, no tumor. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a combination—pain, nausea, vomiting, maybe mild dehydration. Your blood sugar was 146, so not too high or low. We’re watching it closely since you have diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to keep food down, but it’s hard with the gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re going to keep you on IV fluids for now and start you on a PCA pump for pain—dilaudid. It’s stronger and you can control it better, given your tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. If you can keep fluids down, your pain improves, and no fever returns, we may switch to oral meds and send you home in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Pain’s not as bad. I even kept down some apple juice and passed gas. Bowel movement this morning too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to stop the PCA and switch you to oral pain meds. How’s your head? Any dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dizziness. But last night, I saw these little men—like tiny figures—stabbing me and following me. I know it’s not real, but it scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I remember that note. We gave you a low dose of Haldol. It helped, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they went away. Is that from the pain meds? Or my bipolar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be a mix. Pain, stress, being in the hospital—can trigger hallucinations, especially with your history. We’ll keep an eye on it and avoid sedating meds if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober for years, but sometimes I wonder if my brain’s just… worn out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot—chronic pain, surgeries, mental health challenges. But you’re stable now. We’re managing everything step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are better. White count is coming down, no signs of infection. We’re going to start you on your regular meds by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Including my Geodon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart Geodon and your other medications. We’ll also continue monitoring your blood sugar. Your diabetes is still under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the umbilical hernia? It’s been bulging more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It’s not dangerous right now—no obstruction. But you should avoid heavy lifting. We’ll refer you to surgery for evaluation when you’re fully recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. You’ve been off IVs, eating, and your pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you develop high fever, severe pain, vomiting that won’t stop, or pass out again, come back right away. Also, keep an eye on your incisions for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hallucinations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If they come back, call your psychiatrist. But they were likely due to the hospital stress and pain. You should be okay at home with your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow up with your doctors, and we’ll see how you’re doing in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another MRI or CT soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The imaging showed nothing urgent. We’ll repeat only if symptoms change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s been acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw a small hemangioma on your spine—benign, not causing issues. Keep managing it with your usual methods: heat, stretching, and avoid heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my cholesterol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still high, but we’re not changing meds now. Focus on diet and your follow-up with primary care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my seizure history. Should I see neurology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the syncopal episode and possible pseudoseizures, yes—follow up with them. They may want to adjust your management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll make the call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll send your discharge papers and prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Rest, take your meds, and don’t push yourself too hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, gastroparesis, bipolar disorder, and recent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and appendectomy presented with syncope, reported seizure-like activity, and persistent right-sided abdominal pain with vomiting and fever. He was admitted for evaluation and management. Imaging showed no acute intracranial pathology, a small postoperative fluid collection, and mild bile duct dilation without retained stones.
